---

For twenty years I have lived within half a mile of it. I can locate it by orienting west toward the black iron weather-hen, half-strangled with clematis, perched upon the garage roof. Beyond a low ridge in the cliff face of a limestone dale, there lies a cave hidden among the bushes. Long after the old tigers had vanished, leaving only their teeth behind, the people of the valley would climb to that place bearing the dead they deemed most useful. They would push them well inside, then draw them out again and walk them about: "They're coming! They're coming!"

We Malagasies cherish our second burials. We hire a band that arrives by van. Once more, when liquefaction is nearly complete, we cradle our beloved in our arms. From the grave-clothes they fall away in gobbets, as dog-food slips from the can. We wrap them anew in fresh, dry linen. They bless our lives with their happiness. We walk them through the valley—dropping here a finger for the god that is a rat or a raven, there a metatarsal to be set beneath the hearth for luck. And what was luck? The afterlife, back then, was reasonably long: nothing so demented as forever, nothing so martial. The afterlife would join the party.

---

outputs.L2:
For two decades now, I've made my home less than half a mile away from it. I can pinpoint its location by heading west toward the black iron weathervane shaped like a hen, the one nearly choked by clematis climbing over the garage roof. Beyond a small ridge in the sheer face of a limestone valley, hidden among the shrubs, lies a cave. Long after the ancient tigers had vanished—though their teeth remained behind—the people of the valley used to make the climb up there, bringing along their dead who they believed still had purpose. They would shove the bodies deep inside, then later pull them back out and parade them about: "Here they come! Here they come!"

We people of Madagascar treasure our second burials. We pay a band to arrive in their van. Once decomposition has nearly run its course, we cradle our beloved dead once more in our embrace. Pieces of them tumble from their burial cloths in chunks, much like dog-food spilling out from a tin. We swaddle them in clean, dry linen. Their joy becomes a blessing upon our own lives. We carry them on a procession around the valley. Here we leave a finger as an offering to the deity that takes the form of a rat or a raven; there we place a foot-bone beneath the hearth to bring good fortune. And what did fortune mean? In those days, the afterlife stretched on for a decent while—nothing insane like eternity, nothing regimented like an army. The afterlife would show up and join the celebration.

# The Cave in the Limestone Dale

For twenty years I have lived near a cave nestled in a limestone dale, and I could lead you to it with my eyes closed. It sits just beyond the old field boundary, marked by a cluster of weathered stones and the crooked hawthorn that leans over its mouth. The nearby landmarks have become so familiar to me that I can locate the entrance precisely, down to the very footfall where the ground begins its gentle descent.

In ancient times, the people of this valley would carry their most valued dead into that cave. They did not slip quietly into the darkness but paraded their beloved through the passages, announcing their arrival to whatever waited within—an act that seemed to bridge the world of the living and the realm of the departed.

Such practices were not unique to this place. Far away, in Madagascar, the Malagasy people observe a tradition known as "second burials." In these rituals, families exhume the decomposed bodies of their loved ones, hold them close once more, and rewrap them tenderly in fresh linen. It is an act of remembrance and reconnection, a refusal to let death sever the bonds of kinship entirely.

During these ceremonies, portions of the deceased were sometimes left behind—offered to the gods or placed in particular spots believed to bring good fortune. The dead, in this way, remained active participants in the fortunes of the living, their remains woven into the fabric of daily hope and superstition.

Yet the afterlife imagined by these old beliefs, though long, was not endless. It lacked the eternal permanence and the militaristic grandeur that later religious concepts would come to promise. These were quieter faiths, bounded and human in scale—a vision of continuation that eventually faded, much like the memory of those who were once carried, celebrated, into the depths of the cave.
outputs.L4:
# Second Burial

There is a limestone cave not far from where I live, its mouth a dark seam in the pale rock, and I find myself returning to it in thought more often than in body. The cave holds water and silence and the slow architecture of time—stalactites forming a drop at a time, calcium laid down over centuries the way a story is laid down over generations. It is a place that keeps things. And keeping things, I have come to understand, is not the same as letting them go.

I have been reading about the Malagasy, and about a custom they practice called *famadihana*—the "turning of the bones." Every so often, according to the demands of dreams or the passage of years, families in Madagascar open the tombs of their ancestors and bring the dead back out into the light. They lift the wrapped bodies from their resting places, rewrap them in fresh silk shrouds, and carry them on their shoulders in a procession that is anything but mournful. There is music. There is dancing. The living speak to the dead, tell them the news, introduce them to children born since the last unwrapping. Then, when the celebration has run its course, the dead are returned to the tomb until the next time they are called.

I want to be honest about what this involves, because there is no tenderness in the world that does not pass through the body. To exhume the dead is to confront decomposition—the sweetish rot, the loosening of flesh from bone, the way a face becomes first a mask and then a structure and then, at last, only architecture, like the cave. These are not sanitized rituals. The hands that carry the ancestors touch what remains, and what remains is not always beautiful in the way we ask the beautiful to be. And yet the gesture is one of the most tender I can imagine: to hold the disintegrating thing that was once a mother, a grandfather, a child, and to hold it not with horror but with love, and even with joy.

This is what unsettles me and moves me at once. We in the West have built our afterlife elsewhere—up in a distant heaven or down in a punitive hell, in any case *away*, somewhere the dead cannot be visited and cannot visit us. Our dead are sealed behind stone and granite and the polite fiction that they have gone on to a better place. We do not disturb them. We call this respect, but I wonder if it is not also a kind of exile—for them, and for us. The eternal reward we imagine is strangely lonely: an endless, changeless somewhere, cut off from the ongoing life of the family, the village, the world.

The Malagasy vision offers something different. In it, the dead are not banished into an abstract forever. They remain part of the community—consulted, celebrated, carried in the arms of those who loved them. Death is not a door that closes but a threshold crossed and recrossed, a relationship that continues rather than a severance that must be endured. The afterlife, in this understanding, is not somewhere else. It is here, among us, present and joyful, renewed each time the tomb is opened and the silk is unwound and rewound around the beloved bones.

I think of the cave again, and of everything it keeps. Perhaps we ask the wrong question when we ask where the dead go. Perhaps the better question is how we keep them near—how we carry them, and let them decompose in our hands without letting them decompose in our memory. There is comfort in this, a comfort I did not expect to find in the turning of the bones: the possibility that to be dead is not to be gone, and that love, like limestone, has a way of holding on.
outputs.L5:
# The West and the Weight of the Past

There is a particular kind of longing that surfaces **when** we turn our eyes toward the **West**. Perhaps it is the setting sun, dropping below the horizon each evening, that reminds us of endings, of things concluding, of the day slipping into the **past**.

The **West** has always carried a symbolic power in human imagination. In countless cultures, it represents the land of the departed, the direction of the dying light, the frontier beyond which the known world dissolves into mystery. **When** ancient people watched the sun vanish westward, they imagined it descending into another realm, a place where yesterdays gathered and memories dwelled.

## Remembering What Came Before

The **past** is not a fixed thing. It shifts and reshapes itself depending on **when** we choose to look back and what we hope to find there. The American **West**, for instance, lives in memory as a place of wild possibility—of cowboys, open plains, and endless horizons. Yet the reality was always more complicated than the legend, filled with hardship and conflict that the romantic retelling often smooths away.

**When** we romanticize any era, we risk forgetting its darker truths. The **past** deserves honesty as much as affection.

## Looking Forward by Looking Back

There is wisdom in remembering. **When** we understand where we have been, we better navigate where we are going. The **West** may symbolize the end of a day, but every sunset promises a sunrise. The **past** teaches, warns, and inspires—but it should never imprison us.

So let us honor the **past** without living inside it, and let us walk toward the **West** knowing that endings are simply the doorway to what comes next.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic, stream-of-consciousness piece that blends a specific rural English landscape with the Malagasy tradition of famadihana (the turning of the bones), meditating on second burials and what "luck" and the afterlife once meant.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Turning

Somewhere in the wet green throat of Devon, where the hedgerows hold the road like cupped hands holding rain, I am thinking of my grandmother's grave and how we left her there, once, finally, as if *finally* were a word the earth agreed to.

But in the highlands of Madagascar they do not agree.

*

Here the sheep move like slow clouds pulled to ground, and the drystone walls—dear god the labour in them, each stone a decision, each gap a small forgetting—run their grey seams down toward the combe where mist collects like breath. My people buried and turned away. We are good at turning away. We call it respect, this leaving-be, this letting the wet Devon clay close its mouth over the ones we loved and swallow, swallow.

*

Famadihana.

Say it and the syllables unwrap a shroud. Every seven years, or five, or when the ancestor comes walking through a dream complaining of the cold—*I am cold, I am cold, why have you left me to the cold*—the family gathers. They lift the dead. They carry them out into the light that the dead have not seen since last they were danced. New silk. The old cloth crumbling. And they *dance*, they lift the wrapped bones shoulder-high and turn them beneath the sun, laughing, telling them the news—*your granddaughter married, the rice was thin this year, your brother's son has gone to the city and does not write*—

as if death were only a long absence from the table.

*

Would you come back, Gran, if I unearthed you?
Would you complain of the Devon damp, the way you always did in life,
pulling your cardigan tight against the valley's ancient chill?

*

We buried luck once, here, though we've forgotten it. Left milk in saucers. Nailed the horseshoe up—points to the sky so the luck won't spill. Turned our coins at the new moon. Threw the salt. The land remembers what the people shed: the old propitiations, the small negotiations with the dark, the sense that the dead were *near*, were owed, were watching from the barrow on the hill where the bronze folk laid their loved ones with a pot, a pin, a joint of meat—provisions for a road we no longer believe in.

*

There, in the red laterite, the ancestors are wealth. The *razana*. They are the ones who send the rain or hold it. Bless the womb or bar it. Luck is not chance there; luck is *relationship*. Luck is whether you have kept the covenant, whether you have lifted them into the sun and let them feel how much they are still loved, still spoken of, still *turned*.

And here we let our luck grow cold beneath the yews.

*

The combe fills with evening. A blackbird unspools its liquid grief across the fields and I am thinking: what is a second burial but a second chance to say the thing we didn't say—

that we are sorry,
that we remember,
that the rice was thin but we thought of you,
that the house is smaller now with all this quiet in it.

*

To turn the bones is to refuse the lie of *finally*.

*

I stand at the wall's edge where the last light pools like something poured. The dead are down there in the dark of every country, patient in their wrapping, and somewhere a family is dancing its grandmother across a threshing floor beneath a sky riotous with stars, singing, telling her everything, telling her *you are not gone, you are only turned, you are only waiting for the next unwrapping into light*—

and here the mist comes up
and here the sheep bed down against the cold
and here I do not dig,

I only stand
and feel the whole green weight of England
lying still upon its unturned dead,

and I think: *I am cold.*
*I am cold.*
*Why have we left them to the cold.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose poem narrated by someone who has lived near a limestone dale for twenty years, connecting a hidden cave used for ancient burials to the Madagascar custom of exhuming and dancing with the dead.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Turning of the Bones**

Twenty years I have kept this valley, and twenty years the dale has kept its dead.

You would not find the cave unless I showed you—and I will not show you. The mouth is a seam in the limestone, low and green-lipped, where the water has spent ten thousand patient years unbuttoning the hill. I found it in my second autumn, following a fox that had no wish to be followed. Inside, the dark is old the way milk is old, gone thick and strange, and when my lamp first touched the far wall I understood I was not the first to come with fire into that room.

They had lain down their people here. You can feel it before you can prove it—the deliberate arrangement of a threshold, the sense of a house rather than a hole. Later the archaeologists came with their brushes and their careful string, and they told me what I already knew in the soles of my feet: Neolithic, they said. Four thousand years. Bones stacked with intention, skulls set apart, the long bones bundled like kindling for a fire no one meant to light.

*Left*, I thought. *Abandoned.* And for years that word sat sour in me, because who abandons their mother to the limestone dark and walks away up into the light?

Then I read of Madagascar. Of the *famadihana*, the turning of the bones. How every few years the highland families open the tombs and lift their dead into the sun, unwrap the old silk and wrap them in new, and carry them shoulder-high through the village. How they dance. How they tell the grandmother the news—the marriages, the harvests, the child who has her chin. How they do not weep, or not only weep, because the dead are not gone but only *elsewhere*, only *waiting*, only in need of company and a fresh cloth against the cold.

And I understood, standing in my kitchen with the rain on the glass, that I had misread my own valley for eighteen years.

They did not abandon this cave. They *visited* it.

Think of it. The bundled bones, unbundled and bundled again. The skulls moved, arranged, moved once more—not the tidiness of forgetting but the fussing of the living, the way you straighten a sleeping child's blanket though the child will never know. They came back. Down through the green seam with their fire, and they lifted their people, and they said whatever the dead need to be told, and then they laid them down and climbed again into the wind.

I have no proof of this. I have twenty years and a fox and the particular way the dark in that cave does not feel empty.

Now when the light goes long in the dale, and the limestone glows like something newly lifted from the ground, I find I am not afraid of the seam in the hill. I think of the highland families, half a world and forty centuries adrift from these unnamed dead, doing the same tender, impossible thing: refusing the loneliness of the buried. Carrying the ones they love back into the day. Telling them the news.

Twenty years I have kept this valley. When my own turn comes, let someone open the ground on occasion. Let them wrap me warm. Let them tell me who was born, and who the child resembles, and whether the fox still runs the hill that will not be followed.

Then let them lay me down, and dance, and climb back into the light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental piece about death rituals across cultures that shifts from an English valley with a cave and a weathervane to a first-person Malagasy voice describing re-wrapping decomposing loved ones and carrying them around the village.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Weathervane Knows

*

In the English valley the rain comes sideways, and the church has a weathervane shaped like a cockerel, verdigris-green, and it turns.

It turns.

Below it: the cave. Not a proper cave, the locals say, more a hollow in the limestone where the hill opens its one grey eye. In the seventeenth century they laid plague-dead there because the churchyard was full and the ground was frozen and the living could not bear to keep the dead among them, breathing that air.

Now schoolchildren come with clipboards. They shade their eyes. They ask: *is it haunted, miss?* And the teacher, who is tired, who has a mortgage, who has not thought about death since her own father went quiet in a hospice the colour of weak tea, says: *no, of course not, it's just geology.*

Just geology. The bones long removed, catalogued, boxed in the county archive. Handled with cotton gloves. Death made archival. Death made tidy.

The weathervane turns. The cockerel points now to the north, where the wind has decided to come from, and the valley holds its dead the way the English hold most things—

at arm's length,

behind glass,

*don't touch.*

*

*

*

Now I will tell you how we do it, my grandmother's people, on the high red island where the earth is the colour of old blood and the ancestors are not gone, only quieter, only waiting to be asked.

It is the season. The rice is in. The astrologer has spoken and the day is good, and so we open the tomb.

You who have never done this—you flinch. I know. You imagine horror. But listen. This is *famadihana*, the turning of the bones, and it is the happiest day, it is a wedding day, it is the day my grandfather comes back into the sun.

We go down into the tomb where the cold lives. We bring them up, the wrapped ones, the *razana*, our dead. My uncle. My grandmother's sister. My grandfather, who I lift with my own two hands.

He is light. He is so light now, lighter than the child I carried on my hip last summer.

The old silk has gone to lace, has gone to almost-nothing, and beneath it—yes. Yes. He is not what he was. The body does what the body does in the dark and the years. There is a smell that is not a smell you will understand, that lives in the back of the throat, that is grief and earth and something sweet gone wrong and something that is simply *my grandfather now.*

I do not turn my face away.

We wrap him in new silk, the *lambamena*, the good cloth, red-golden, that cost my father three months' wages, and it is *worth it*, do you hear me, it is worth everything—

and then we lift him,

and we dance.

We carry him around the tomb, around and around, the band playing, the trumpets bright and cracked, and I am laughing, I am weeping, I hold his shoulders that are hardly shoulders and I *tell* him things—

*Grandfather, my daughter can read now. Grandfather, the western field flooded. Grandfather, do you remember, do you remember, do you—*

We carry them through the village. We hold them up so they can see. See how the rice grows. See who has married. See how we go on, and how you go on with us, because you are not *gone*, you are only *ahead*, you have only walked a little further up the same road—

*

The English teacher, five thousand miles north, tells the children to line up.

The cockerel turns to the east.

She does not know that somewhere the dead are dancing. She only knows the cave is empty and the bones are boxed and the day is cold, and she thinks, without knowing why, of her father's hand going slack in hers, and how no one had told her what to *do* with it—

with the hand,

with the love,

with the enormous unspent tenderness that had nowhere, suddenly, to go.

*

We put them back at last, when the sun is low. Back into the cool dark, wrapped warm and new, and we seal the tomb, and we go home to eat and drink and be loud with living.

But we are not sad. Why would we be sad?

We will come back.

That is the whole of it, the thing your cave has forgotten, the thing your green rooster cannot say though it turns and turns and turns:

*we will come back for them.*

We always come back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a lyrical meditation on ancestor worship and second burials, mixing vivid decay imagery with reflections on how the afterlife used to be "fairly long" but not eternal or militarized.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Second Death

There was a time the dead did not stay dead
in the way we mean it now—
that sharp cliff-edge, that final door.
No. They *lingered.*

They dwelt in the loam a while,
becoming soft, becoming honest.
The flesh unclasped itself from bone
like a hand releasing a coin it had gripped too long,
and this was not an ending
but a **loosening.**

---

We buried them once, and waited.

Let the earth do its slow arithmetic—
the beetle's tithe, the fungal bloom,
the marrow gone to sweetness,
then to nothing sweet at all.
We knew the timeline of a body
the way we knew the sowing months.
*First rot, then patience, then return.*

And when the bones came clean,
we dug them up again—
this was the **second burial,**
the true one, the one that mattered.
We washed the skull like a beloved cup.
We spoke to it. We fed it.
We carried it inside the house of belonging.

---

Back then the afterlife was **fairly long**
but not forever—
this is the part we've forgotten how to hold.

No eternal fire.
No eternal reward.
No legions of the saved,
no armies of the damned marching under banners,
no cosmic war dressed up as comfort.

Just a *while.*
A generous while.
The dead stayed as long as someone remembered
their laugh, their grudge, the way they salted bread.
Three generations, maybe four—
then even the ghost grew tired,
lay down inside forgetting,
and was permitted, at last, to be *done.*

---

We made the dead into ancestors
the way we make wine from spoiling fruit:
by trusting the decay,
by refusing to look away from it,
by naming corruption
the **first step home.**

They rotted so that they could ripen.
They fell apart so we could gather them.

---

Now we seal our dead in polished boxes,
pump them full of chemicals against the honest work,
and demand of them an *eternity*—
as if we could not bear
that anything might simply, gently, cease.

We gave the afterlife a border and a sword.
We made it permanent, and thereby made it cruel.
We forgot the mercy of the second death:
that even ghosts deserve
a place to finally lie down.

---

So let me be buried twice.
Let me go soft in the ground and be forgotten *slowly.*
Let someone lift my clean bones into the light,
speak my name a few more turns of season—
and then let even that release its grip.

Not eternal.
Not enlisted in any war.

Just **long enough.**
Just held, then loam,
then the deep and dreamless
generosity of being through.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Craft a dark, tender poem about reburial customs—part memory of an English limestone cave where the dead were walked among the living, part account of the Malagasy famadihana with its hired band and bones dropped for gods.
counterfactuals.output:
**Second Earth**

*I.*
There was a cave once, in the soft stone country,
where we did not leave the dead to be strangers.
Limestone keeps its dead like letters in a drawer—
folded, cool, the ink of them not yet run.

We went down with candles to visit.
Grandmother in her niche, the small
white architecture of her hands still praying.
We told her the weather, the marriages,
the price of wheat, and walked the aisles of ancestors
as through a market at first light, quiet, familiar,
touching a jaw, a cup of pelvis,
the way you'd touch a gatepost coming home.

The living need the dead to stay a while
in the room of the visible. Grief is only love
that has misplaced its body.

*II.*
On the far island they know this, and answer it with brass.
Every seven years the tombs are opened,
the band hired—accordion, drum, a trumpet
gone green at the mouth—and the dead are lifted
into a light they have forgotten,
wrapped and rewrapped in clean silk,
white as the first idea of them.

They dance. The family dances the bones
shoulder-high, laughing, weeping, careless-tender,
because a bone that is danced is a bone that is loved,
and love is the only proof against forgetting.

Then, before the sun can set them down again,
they raise the ancestors high and let them fall
a little—a spill of femur, a rattle of ribs—
an offering flung up to the gods:
*here, take our best, our dearest ruined furniture,
and send it back as rain, as rice, as children.*

*III.*
Both are one tenderness in different weather.
We cannot bear to bury love at once.
We give it a second earth, a second music—
the drip of stone, the drop of bone,
the long conversation we keep having
with the mouths that have stopped answering,
and answer still, in us, who are their turning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
